description: Article 101 TFEU contains the prohibition in paragraph (1) against anticompetitive agreements
Article 101 TFEU contains the exemption mechanism in paragraph (3)
Agreements caught by Art.101(1) may be exempted under Art.101(3) if four cumulative conditions are met
Articles 101 and 102 are the twin pillars of EU competition law — agreements vs unilateral conduct
Regulation 1/2003 implements the enforcement regime for Article 101 TFEU
Regulation 1/2003 implements the enforcement regime for Article 102 TFEU
Regulation 1/2003 established the European Competition Network for decentralised enforcement
Regulation 1/2003 empowers NCAs to directly apply Articles 101 and 102 in full
Regulation 1/2003 Art.9 establishes the commitment decision procedure
VBER provides a block exemption from Art.101(1) for qualifying vertical agreements
VBER defines the safe harbour framework for assessing vertical restraints
VBER Art.4 lists hardcore restrictions that remove the entire agreement from block exemption
VBER treats resale price maintenance as a hardcore restriction excluded from the block exemption
VBER provides specific rules for selective distribution systems including online sales restrictions
HBER provides block exemptions from Art.101(1) for qualifying horizontal cooperation agreements
Horizontal cooperation guidelines accompanying HBER provide detailed guidance on information exchange
EUMR Art.3 defines the concept of concentration (merger, acquisition of control, full-function JV)
EUMR Art.1 sets out the turnover thresholds defining EU dimension
EUMR Art.2 establishes the SIEC test as the substantive standard for merger assessment
EUMR requires mandatory pre-notification and clearance for concentrations with EU dimension
EUMR Art.7 establishes the standstill obligation; breach constitutes gun-jumping
EUMR Art.22 allows Member States to refer below-threshold concentrations to the Commission
EUMR Art.4(5) allows parties to request pre-notification referral to the Commission
EUMR Art.9 allows referral of concentrations from the Commission to a Member State NCA
Phase I review is the first stage of the merger notification process
Phase II in-depth investigation follows if Phase I raises serious doubts
Phase II is opened when Phase I review identifies serious doubts about compatibility
The SIEC test requires prior definition of the relevant product and geographic markets
Efficiencies may be considered in the SIEC assessment to offset competitive harm
The failing firm defence provides a counterfactual argument within the SIEC assessment
The SIEC test assesses whether the merger creates or strengthens market power
The SSNIP test is the standard methodology for defining the relevant market
Market power assessment depends on prior definition of the relevant market
Art.102 requires a finding of dominance (significant market power) as a prerequisite
Self-preferencing by dominant platforms may constitute abuse under Art.102
Tying and bundling by dominant undertakings may constitute abuse under Art.102(d)
Predatory pricing by dominant undertakings constitutes abuse under Art.102
Margin squeeze by vertically integrated dominant firms constitutes abuse under Art.102
Art.102 analysis requires definition of the relevant market to assess dominance
Art.101(1) distinguishes between restrictions by object and by effect
De minimis doctrine limits Art.101(1) to agreements that appreciably restrict competition
Cartels are the most serious infringement of the Art.101(1) prohibition
Art.101(1) covers concerted practices as well as formal agreements
Cartel conduct (price-fixing, market sharing) constitutes hardcore restrictions
The leniency programme is the primary tool for detecting and prosecuting cartels
Dawn raids are a key investigative tool for gathering evidence of cartel conduct
The settlement procedure offers a streamlined resolution pathway for cartel cases
Fines for cartel infringements are calculated using the 2006 Guidelines methodology
Cartels are treated as restrictions by object — no proof of anticompetitive effects required
Exchange of competitively sensitive information may constitute or evidence a concerted practice
Hub-and-spoke arrangements are a form of indirect concerted practice between competitors
Hub-and-spoke conspiracies involve indirect information exchange through a common trading partner
Leniency applicant evidence often triggers or supports dawn raid inspections
Leniency and settlement reductions are cumulative — first leniency applicant can also settle
Leniency reductions are applied to the fine calculated under the fining guidelines methodology
DG Competition enforces Article 101 TFEU on anticompetitive agreements
DG Competition enforces Article 102 TFEU on abuse of dominant position
DG Competition reviews and decides on mergers under the EU Merger Regulation
DG Competition enforces state aid rules under Articles 107-109 TFEU
DG Competition enforces the Digital Markets Act gatekeeper obligations
DG Competition conducts dawn raid inspections as part of its investigative powers
NCAs are members of the European Competition Network alongside the Commission
The Commission (DG Competition) coordinates the ECN
ECN+ Directive empowers NCAs with harmonised enforcement tools and independence guarantees
ECN+ Directive strengthens the effectiveness of the European Competition Network
Damages Directive enables private enforcement of Art.101 through damages actions
Damages Directive enables private enforcement of Art.102 through damages actions
The General Court reviews Commission competition decisions on appeal
The CJEU hears appeals on points of law from the General Court
Structural remedies (divestitures) are typically offered during Phase II to address competition concerns
Behavioural remedies may be accepted in Phase II alongside or instead of structural measures
Parties may offer structural commitments in Phase I to obtain clearance without Phase II
Structural remedies are generally preferred over behavioural remedies in merger cases
The DMA defines the gatekeeper designation criteria and process
The DMA defines the 10 categories of core platform services subject to regulation
DMA Art.5 sets out the self-executing obligations for designated gatekeepers
DMA Art.6 sets out obligations susceptible to further specification
DMA Art.7 establishes interoperability obligations for messaging services
The DMA explicitly prohibits self-preferencing by gatekeepers in ranking and data use
The DMA complements Art.102 with ex-ante regulation of gatekeeper platforms
Art.108 establishes the notification and review procedures for state aid under Art.107
Art.109 empowers the Council to adopt implementing regulations for Arts.107-108
Art.109 TFEU is the legal basis for GBER, the general block exemption for state aid
GBER declares certain categories of state aid compatible with Art.107, exempting from notification
Art.108 empowers the Commission to order recovery of unlawful and incompatible state aid
FSR notification obligations apply alongside EUMR for concentrations involving foreign subsidies
FSR extends state aid-like scrutiny to subsidies granted by non-EU countries
Fining guidelines methodology applies to infringements of Art.101
Fining guidelines methodology applies to infringements of Art.102
